title: To the edge of the cliff (Luke 4:22–30)
hookLine: his own town loves him, then tries to throw him off a cliff, and he walks through them

cards: "Is not this Joseph's son?" It's said in the same synagogue, a minute after the reading, and at first it sounds proud. Luke says they "wondered at the gracious words which proceeded out of his mouth."
The hometown boy, all grown up. You can almost hear the aunties. But hometowns are complicated.
The same people who love you also think they know exactly who you are, and what you owe them. We've heard what you did in Capernaum, they're thinking. Do it here.
Within a few verses, this warm room becomes a crowd marching him to the edge of a hill.

teach.b: Jesus names what they're thinking: "Ye will surely say unto me this proverb, Physician, heal thyself." Then: "Verily I say unto you, No prophet is accepted in his own country."
And he reaches for two stories from their own scriptures.

teach.h: A WIDOW IN SIDON, A SYRIAN GENERAL.
teach.b: In the days of Elijah there was a famine, and many widows in Israel, but the prophet was sent to a widow in Sarepta, in the region of Sidon, outside Israel.
In the days of Elisha there were many lepers in Israel, "and none of them was cleansed, saving Naaman the Syrian." A foreign widow. A foreign general.
Both showing God's care reaching past the expected circle. That turns the room.

teach.h: FILLED WITH WRATH, TO THE BROW OF THE HILL.
teach.b: "All they in the synagogue, when they heard these things, were filled with wrath," and it moves fast: they "thrust him out of the city, and led him unto the brow of the hill whereon their city was built, that they might cast him down headlong."
This isn't about one town being worse than others. It's something any group can do: love the prophet until the prophet says God's kindness isn't only ours.

teach.h: THROUGH THE MIDST, AND ON HIS WAY.
teach.b: Then the ending, so quiet you can miss it: "But he passing through the midst of them went his way." No miracle is described. No fight, no speech, no running.

teach.h: HE PASSING THROUGH THE MIDST OF THEM WENT HIS WAY.
teach.b: He walks through the crowd and keeps going. Luke doesn't explain how, and the silence is part of the picture: the anger doesn't get to decide his direction.

how: Some Christians read the rejection at Nazareth as a picture of how hard it is to hear a prophet close to home, and Nazareth has a traditional hilltop site linked to the story.

o: Greek for a prophet sent to foreigners
Greek for the brow of a hill or cliff
Greek for homeland, your own hometown

games.q: what's inside Luke 4:22–30 — tap the pairs.
p: sent to a widow in Sidon

s: the people of Nazareth were angry from the first word
they first wondered at his gracious words.
his two examples came from Israel's own prophets
Elijah and Elisha, from the books of Kings.
Luke describes a miracle that freed him from the crowd
he simply passed through the midst of them and went his way. Luke doesn't explain how.

games.q: your own town is pushing you toward the edge of a hill. what do you do?
o: give them the miracle they want.
pass through the middle of them and go your way.
argue until they agree with you.
games.why: he walks through the crowd and keeps going. no fight and no explanation: the anger doesn't decide his direction.

practice: Remember a time when people who liked you suddenly didn't, a group chat gone cold, a family dinner that soured, praise that flipped into blame, and notice whether it still shows up in your body.

Then picture Jesus at the brow of the hill, walking steadily through, no shouting, no pleading, and breathe slowly while your shoulders drop. If you pray, ask for that steadiness; if not, simply practice the slow breath.

wordCard.voice: Patris, Greek for homeland, hometown: his own town wonders at him, then turns on him, and he walks through the middle of them.

orig.note: Greek: homeland, home town. no prophet is accepted in his own patris.

carryVoice: Your line: he went his way. Not fighting the crowd, and not obeying it. That's day five hundred seventeen.
